item.title: Trump Has Tried to Ban Reporters From Government Spaces Before
item.description:
The Trump administration has repeatedly moved to ban reporters from the White House and other government property.

In January 2025, Mr. Trump tried to bar Associated Press journalists from parts of the White House, including the Oval Office and Air Force One. The A.P. has sued to restore its access, but that case remains in litigation; in the meantime, A.P. photographers have had continued access to the Oval Office. Its print journalists have had more limited access.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has also placed limits on reporters’ access to the Pentagon, including a requirement that all journalists be accompanied by an official escort while in the building. The Pentagon also closed the work space used for years by journalists with credentials to cover the military. The New York Times sued over the restrictions, and the litigation continues.

During his first term, Mr. Trump revoked a White House pass for Jim Acosta, the former CNN journalist. CNN succeeded in restoring Mr. Acosta’s press credentials in court.

Mr. Trump also tried to temporarily suspend the press pass of a reporter who traded caustic comments with Sebastian Gorka, a right-wing commentator who worked briefly in the White House. The reporter successfully sued to restore his credential.

item.title: Appeals Court Restricts Trump Administration Deportation Effort
item.description:
The Trump administration will face new requirements before it is allowed to deport people to countries other than their nation of origin, an appeals court ruled on Friday.

The ruling, by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, requires that immigrants facing deportation to so-called third countries be given more due process beforehand — “a meaningful opportunity” to raise fears of persecution or torture. In a 55-page opinion with no dissent, a three-judge panel from the court rejected arguments from the Trump administration that it receives “assurances” from foreign governments that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured and that such communications should be sufficient.

The administration’s current policy “conflicts” with laws and regulations that protect detainees from torture, the judges ruled, and added that they were rejecting an attempt by the Homeland Security Department to carve out an exception to those rules “from whole cloth.”

If the ruling remains in place, it will impose a substantial and time-consuming hurdle on Mr. Trump’s third-country deportation program. The practice of sending deportees to faraway and sometimes dangerous countries, often with just a few hours’ notice, has been one of the administration’s highest-profile attempts to create uncertainty for immigrants already in the United States.

The administration has sent migrants to nations including South Sudan, Liberia and Equatorial Guinea as part of the program. In interviews with The New York Times, some migrants deported to third countries have made harrowing allegations that they were abused by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The Homeland Security Department has said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” while in ICE custody, and denied that anyone has been beaten or tortured.

In March, the appeals panel temporarily blocked a ruling by Judge Brian E. Murphy of Massachusetts imposing the new requirements. Friday’s order lifts that block, putting most of the new legal hurdles to third-country deportations into place.

The administration can now appeal the ruling to a larger First Circuit panel or to the Supreme Court.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The case already reached the Supreme Court last year, when the justices agreed to allow eight men who had been sent to Djibouti in violation of a preliminary order from Judge Murphy to be sent onward to South Sudan. That ruling dealt with the issue on a temporary basis, while litigation over it moved forward.

The appeals court on Friday struck down one of the requirements that Judge Murphy had attempted to impose on D.H.S. Judge Murphy would have required the department to prioritize deportees’ home countries as destinations, but the appeals court said that could not be legally mandated.

In a statement, Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the migrants who brought the lawsuit, called Friday’s ruling “a major victory for the basic principle that the government cannot deport people to an unknown country without first telling them where they are being sent and giving them a meaningful opportunity to explain why they would face persecution or torture there.”

The unanimous opinion was written by Judge Seth R. Aframe, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Also on the panel were Judge Jeffrey R. Howard, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, and Judge Lara E. Montecalvo, another appointee of Mr. Biden. Judge Murphy is also a Biden appointee.

item.title: Trump Won Their Votes. Now His Trade War Is Dividing Them.
item.description:
President Trump’s decision to escalate a trade war with Canada is threatening to hurt Republicans in the midterm elections, with several Senate battleground states on the northern border feeling an outsize impact.

Many voters say they are upset about the trade war, including some who cast ballots for Mr. Trump in 2024 with hopes that he would bring them relief from rising prices, according to more than four dozen interviews across six states at the center of the battle for control of the Senate.

The intensifying trade conflict — touching steel, dairy, appliances, automotive parts and agricultural equipment — has forced some Republicans to play defense. Democrats have highlighted the costs of the trade fight, which has spooked financial markets and threatened to accelerate inflation driven by Mr. Trump’s unpopular war with Iran.

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican, has pushed Mr. Trump to de-escalate the trade war. In Michigan, the Republican nominee for Senate, Mike Rogers, has appeared to stand uneasily with Mr. Trump’s trade policy.

Nationwide, 78 percent of likely midterm voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 still supported his trade policies, but 19 percent oppose them, according to the latest poll from The New York Times and Siena University. The poll did not ask voters specifically about the trade war with Canada.

The impact of the trade war is felt acutely in states that are along the northern border or have heavily industrial and agricultural economies that make them reliant on trade with Canada — characteristics shared by some of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds.

In interviews in Alaska, Minnesota, Michigan, Maine, New Hampshire and Ohio, many voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 said they believed the president was leveling the playing field with his trade war. But others said the fight with an ally was a mistake.

Candace Oxley, 80, of Kettering, Ohio. Ms. Oxley, a retiree, said that she was dismayed by the trade conflict and that Mr. Trump was preoccupied by vanity projects. His fight with Canada, she said, is not helping Americans afford groceries or gas. “I voted for him, and I wish I had not,” Ms. Oxley said. She said she was unsure how she would vote in Ohio’s competitive Senate race between Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat.

Shkelqim Doko, 65, of Sterling Heights, Mich. Mr. Doko, a bakery owner, said he supported Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, arguing that the president was working to get even with countries that have taken advantage of the United States. “I stand by my vote,” Mr. Doko said of his support for Mr. Trump in 2024, adding that he sees Mr. Trump as “pro-America.” Mr. Doko said he would vote for Mr. Rogers, the Republican nominee in Michigan’s high-stakes Senate race, because Mr. Rogers would support Mr. Trump’s trade policies. “If we trade,” Mr. Doko said, “we trade in balance.”

Elaine Flowers, 75, of Sterling Heights, Mich. Ms. Flowers, a retired social worker and onetime police officer, expressed hope that the trade war would have long-term benefits. “I just don’t see a good life for my grandkids if we don’t get the industries back in the United States,” Ms. Flowers said. A former Democrat, Ms. Flowers said she now identified as an independent. She said Mr. Trump was the first Republican she voted for after leaving the Democratic Party. She plans to vote for Mr. Rogers in the Senate race in Michigan, she said.

Ben Rackliff, 53, of Jefferson, Maine. Mr. Rackliff, a contractor, said he opposed the trade war and that it had affected his business. “It’s not the presidency I voted for,” said Mr. Rackliff, adding that the president was taking his tariffs “to an extreme.” Still, Mr. Rackliff said he planned to vote for Ms. Collins, a moderate Republican, over the Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson, a former State Senate president. “Whether she’s a RINO or whatever they want to call her, she is present, she does go to the votes,” Mr. Rackliff, using an acronym for Republican in name only, said of Ms. Collins. “She does, for the most part, represent Maine.”

Jonathon Stevens, 24, of Grafton, N.H. Mr. Stevens, a carpenter, said he had voted for Mr. Trump because of his tax policies and what he believed was Mr. Trump’s “blue-collar” approach. But Mr. Stevens said that he was dismayed by Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada, and that he missed former President Barack Obama’s “professionalism.” The United States and Canada are “too close” to be on bad terms, said Mr. Stevens, who considers himself a political independent. He is uncertain who he will vote for in the midterms, he said, but he is leaning toward supporting Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, in the Senate race in New Hampshire.

Stephen Tolan, 63, of Anchorage. Mr. Tolan, a surveyor, said that while the trade war had costs, he ultimately felt Mr. Trump had to ratchet up the tariffs on Canada. “I believe Canada’s been overcharging us for years,” Mr. Tolan said. He added: “Canada’s been living under our umbrella for 250 years. They need to pay up.” Mr. Tolan said he was supporting Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska because the incumbent “backs up Trump.” Mr. Sullivan faces a stiff midterm challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

Bennett Coughlan, 34, of Mankato, Minn. Mr. Coughlan, who owns a coffee shop, said that he was generally skeptical of government interference in trade, but that he could accept the use of tariffs with a “clear objective and a way to get back to a stable trading relationship.” The trade war with Canada does not seem to fit that description, he said. “You need some confidence that the rules won’t change overnight,” Mr. Coughlan said, questioning whether the United States should “alienate our allies.” Still, Mr. Coughlan said he did not regret voting for Mr. Trump in 2024, suggesting he did not have a good alternative. And he said he was unsure how he would vote in the Senate race in Minnesota, which pits Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against the former N.F.L. sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, a Republican.

Kevin Williams in Ohio, Olivia Gieger in New Hampshire, Julia O’Malley in Alaska, Robb Murray in Minnesota and Murray Carpenter in Maine contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Sherrod Brown Tries a New Retort to Criticism on Transgender Issues
item.description:
Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Ohio, has spent more than $200,000 on a 30-second advertisement responding to attacks from his opponent and an Elon Musk-backed PAC regarding transgender issues, according to AdImpact.

Here’s a look at the ad, its accuracy and its major takeaway.

The ad opens with voters identified as Beth and Warren in Johnstown, Ohio, an agricultural hub just south of Columbus that has historically leaned Republican.

Warren speaks first, looking directly at the camera, and says, “Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown.”

The ad then pans to a voter in Granville, a Democratic island in a conservative part of the state, who says, “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?”

As another voter speaks, a text overlay on an image of a dark, empty hospital hallway reads: “IN OHIO IT’S ILLEGAL TO PERFORM TRANSGENDER SURGERIES ON CHILDREN.”

A series of voters in different parts of the state then denounce Senator Jon Husted, Mr. Brown’s Republican opponent, accusing him of voting to increase the cost of groceries, kicking hundreds of thousands of Ohioans off health care, writing a law letting utility companies “jack up our electric bills,” and failing to address the cost of gas.

The ad ends with Beth in Johnstown, who faces the camera and says “John Husted, why don’t you start working for us?”

Mr. Brown is in a high-stakes race against Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat of JD Vance when he left to become vice president. Mr. Brown has faced a torrent of negative advertising focusing on transgender issues.

“Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown. With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about. In Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right, it’s illegal. Jon Husted, why’d you vote to increase the cost of groceries? To do nothing about the cost of gas. You kicked 490,000 Ohioans off their health care. And Jon Husted wrote the law on letting utility companies jack up our electric bills. Jon Husted, why don’t you start working for us? I’m Sherrod Brown and I approve this message.”

The advertisement is correct that an Ohio law passed in 2024, over the Republican governor’s veto, forbids doctors from prescribing medications that assist minors seeking gender transitions. The law also restricts transgender girls and women from competing in girls and women’s sports.

The law is being challenged before the state Supreme Court, which is made up of six Republican justices and one Democrat.

It is misleading to say that Mr. Husted voted to “increase the cost of groceries,” because there was not a specific vote on that issue in the Senate. But he has supported sweeping tariffs and the war with Iran, among other policies, that have contributed to the rising prices, including of groceries and gas.

Mr. Husted also voted for President Trump’s signature domestic policy bill, which included significant cuts to Medicaid and Medicare. The Joint Economic Committee, a bipartisan group, estimated that more that 489,815 Ohioans would lose health insurance as a result of the cuts.

The claim that Mr. Husted wrote a law that allowed utility companies to raise prices is accurate and complicated. Mr. Husted, then a lieutenant governor, was highly involved in passing a 2019 energy law that later became the center of a massive bribery scheme that landed another lawmaker, the former speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, in prison.

The law allowed utility companies to add extra fees and surcharges to electricity bills as a bailout for two struggling nuclear power plants. Mr. Husted has denied any knowledge of wrongdoing in the high-profile scandal.

This spot represents a new response to the Republican Party’s effort to use transgender issues to paint Democrats as radical and unelectable, regardless of their specific stances, which tend to be more nuanced than portrayed by their opponents.

Instead of engaging on the topic, Mr. Brown’s campaign is seeking to dismiss it as irrelevant, and a distraction from the economic issues that they hope will drive voters to the polls.

item.title: Man Charged in Boy’s Disappearance After 33 Years
item.description:
When 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr. hopped on his bike on May 24, 1993, near his Maryland home, it was the last time his family saw him.

The disappearance of George, who was also known as Junior, shocked Prince George’s County in Maryland and prompted a large manhunt by law enforcement, including the F.B.I. Volunteers also joined the search.

But the case languished for more than 33 years.

Now, investigators say they have arrested a 61-year-old man, Joseph Lynch, who has been charged with second-degree murder, rape and other sexual abuse charges in connection with George’s disappearance.

Another person, a 47-year-old man, whom Mr. Lynch also sexually assaulted, admitted to beating George to death, the authorities said.

That unidentified man has not been charged, the Prince George’s County Police Department said. The county state attorney’s office would not comment on Friday.

“We held onto hope for 33 years,” said Virginia Burdynski, George’s sister, at a news conference on Thursday. “This is not what we prayed for.”

Mr. Lynch appeared in court on Friday and was being held without bail, according to court records. A lawyer representing him could not immediately be reached.

Investigators got a break in the case after a witness, the 47-year-old man, stepped forward in June and said he was with George and Mr. Lynch at the time of the boy’s disappearance.

The witness, who was 13 in 1993, lived in George’s neighborhood.

Mr. Lynch physically and sexually assaulted the witness on the day that George disappeared, according to a statement of charges.

On that same day, Mr. Lynch forced the witness to sexually assault George while Mr. Lynch watched, the statement said.

Mr. Lynch is accused of establishing control over the witness, compelling his participation and standing in a doorway to prevent the witness from leaving, the statement said.

“The witness stated that immediately thereafter, he became extremely angry because of the physical and sexual abuse he had endured from the suspect earlier that morning,” the statement of charges said.

The witness told investigators he could not direct his anger toward Mr. Lynch and instead targeted George, who was younger and smaller, the statement said.

“The witness admitted repeatedly punching and kicking the victim until the victim stopped moving,” the statement said. “The witness recalled observing blood coming from the victim’s head and believed that the victim was dead or had been fatally injured.”

Mr. Lynch retrieved a knife, tarp and rope and rolled George inside, the statement said.

Mr. Lynch and the witness carried George’s body to a location in Prince George’s County and disposed of him, the statement said.

George’s body has never been found.

“Taken together, the suspect’s actions before, during and immediately after the offenses establish that he was an active participant in the continuous course of criminal conduct that resulted in the victim’s death,” the statement.

Mr. Lynch had been previously convicted in 1994 of two sex offenses involving minors, said Chief George R. Nader of the Prince George’s County Police Department.

George was not identified as a victim in that case, the chief said.

Mr. Lynch was sentenced to 20 years in prison and was released in 2006, Chief Nader said.

The chief said he believed there were other victims.

“They have a voice,” he said. “We want to hear from them.”

The testimony of the witness who confessed to killing George may be central to the prosecution’s case, especially if little evidence has survived, said Max Frizalone, a criminal defense lawyer based in Maryland who is not involved in the case.

If the witness invokes his Fifth Amendment right to refuse to incriminate himself by testifying, that could put the prosecution’s case in jeopardy, he said.

Prosecutors may have sought immunity for the witness, Mr. Frizalone said.

“A prosecutor who concluded that the adult directed the killing and that the child acted under his domination would have a coherent reason both to charge Lynch with murder and to use the witness as a witness rather than a defendant,” he said.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

]]>

item.title: A.I. Attack Ads Prompt Police Report in Texas Race
item.description:
The Democratic candidate for Texas lieutenant governor filed a police report on Saturday accusing the Republican incumbent, Dan Patrick, of violating a state law that makes it a crime to produce deepfake videos of political candidates near an election.

The filing centers on two ads released by Mr. Patrick this month that used videos generated by artificial intelligence to depict the Democratic candidate, Vikki Goodwin, describing her policies in words she never said.

“Although the ‘person’ in the video appears to be me, it was not actually me,” Ms. Goodwin, an Austin-area state representative, wrote in an affidavit accompanying the report. “This outrageous behavior by an elected official is criminal.”

Political campaigns around the country have leveraged A.I. to generate attack ads against rival candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. But the filing appeared to be among the few instances of a candidate seeking criminal penalties in response to an A.I. attack.

It was unclear whether Mr. Patrick’s ads were covered by state law, which bars the use of A.I.-generated deepfake videos within 30 days of an election. The ads were posted on Mr. Patrick’s social media accounts during the first two weeks of this month — more than 30 days before Election Day in November.

In the affidavit, Ms. Goodwin argued that the videos violated the law because they remained online within 30 days of the start of early voting.

Allen Blakemore, a campaign spokesman for Mr. Patrick, stood by the video on Saturday, saying it was “an obvious parody produced to entertain.”

“No reasonable person could view it any other way,” Mr. Blakemore said. “Furthermore, we have not published or distributed any of these parodies within 30 days of the election.”

A.I.-generated content has become increasingly common and contentious in political races around the country. As the technology has improved, so has the prevalence of A.I. videos in political ads and social media posts.

This month in Georgia, attacks on the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Jon Ossoff, used an A.I.-generated likeness to show him at a salon getting his hair and nails done. The Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican political action committee, released the ad. Unlike the fabricated depiction of Ms. Goodwin, the A.I.-generated version of Mr. Ossoff does not speak.

In the Senate race in Texas, supporters of Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee, have produced videos depicting an A.I.-generated version of his Democratic opponent, James Talarico. One ad released this month by Mr. Paxton’s campaign uses the fabricated version of Mr. Talarico to deliver a mixture of statements he has made and remarks invented for the video.

Texas is not the only place where political candidates have created videos that include A.I.-generated versions of rivals speaking. For example, in Wisconsin, a Republican congressman, Derrick Van Orden, posted A.I.-generated videos on Facebook last month depicting his Democratic challenger yelling and calling herself “the anointed one.”

In a statement, the Democrat, Rebecca Cooke, called the video “A.I. slop” and said Mr. Van Orden used “A.I. to put words in my mouth because he has nothing else to run on.” A spokeswoman for Mr. Van Orden’s campaign, Grace Kim, said the videos were “obviously AI-generated satire” and were “grounded in reality.”

More than 30 states now have laws regulating the use of deepfakes in political campaigns, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Most require disclosure, while a few, including Maryland, Minnesota and Texas, have adopted prohibitions.

The Texas law, passed in 2019, was among the first to regulate deepfake videos of candidates. At the time, the technology was less accessible and less sophisticated, and such videos were uncommon in political campaigns.

The ads against Ms. Goodwin draw on votes she cast as a state representative. But in an interview, she said her views were distorted in the ads, and she worried that the A.I.-generated images could confuse voters.

“There are a lot of people who don’t know me yet who might think this is me,” she said.

Ms. Goodwin said the Texas law does not go far enough. For example, Texas does not require that campaigns disclose when A.I. was used in an advertisement. An effort to require disclosures passed in the State House last year, but failed in the State Senate, which is overseen by Mr. Patrick. Mr. Patrick’s most recent ad ends with a disclosure that the video “contains digitally generated imagery,” though it does not mention artificial intelligence.

“I have much greater faith in the voters than Ms. Goodwin does,” said Mr. Blakemore, the Patrick spokesman.

It was not immediately clear if or when the police in Austin would open an investigation in response to the report filed by Ms. Goodwin. The department’s automatically generated response, shared with The New York Times, said the report could take five days to process. A police spokesman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Goodwin said she would not use A.I.-generated imagery in her own campaign “because of the issue of data centers.” After filing the police report, she attended a town hall about data centers in San Antonio, according to her campaign.

item.title: Trump Says His Son Will Pay Back Russian Businessman for Wedding Party
item.description:
President Trump on Friday said his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., would pay back a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin who helped finance his wedding after-party in the Bahamas this year, while also defending the payments as “totally allowed.”

“That’s very common; I’ve heard of many people giving wedding parties,” Mr. Trump said, adding, “With all of that being said, I understand that Don has paid him back.”

Mr. Trump’s remarks came after he was asked by a reporter in the Oval Office if it was appropriate for his son to accept the payments of hundreds of thousands of dollars, which disregards the ethical norms for an American president and his family.

Donald Trump Jr. accepted the gifts from Umar Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, according to people with knowledge of the matter. ProPublica earlier reported on the payments, which included the renting of a private island and a fireworks display. His father did not attend the wedding.

Donald Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Trump, previously acknowledged the gifts on social media. They said the trip to the island was not their actual wedding ceremony but rather “an already planned weekend” with friends. Some ethics experts have said that distinction was irrelevant. The couple described their relationship with Mr. Kremlev as a friendship, and said he had not attended the actual wedding ceremony.

Despite the defense of the gifts, Donald Trump Jr. apparently felt it was best to pay the money back, according to Mr. Trump.

“I hear he’s paid him back,” Mr. Trump said. “A person that he knows, I guess a friend of his, they gave him a wedding party.”

Mr. Trump, however, said he was fine with the practice.

“I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people,” Mr. Trump said.

item.title: Newsom Signs Bills Meant to Prevent Trump’s Interference in Midterms
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation on Saturday that is meant to prevent interference in California’s midterm elections in response to efforts by President Trump and other Republicans to restrict voting participation.

Mr. Newsom and fellow Democrats in the State Legislature crafted the bills to broadly combat involvement by the Trump administration, without knowing specifically whether or how the federal government might engage in California’s elections. The state relies heavily on mail ballots, and Mr. Trump has taken particular aim at that form of voting.

One bill prohibits the seizure of ballots, election records or voting technology before an election is certified. Another makes it a felony for people in positions of authority to direct their workers to interfere with the delivery of a mail ballot or its return to election officials.

Mr. Newsom signed a package of 13 bills, including a measure that prohibits arrests within 200 feet of a polling place on Election Day, with exceptions for acts related to disrupting the election or crimes against people or property. Democrats have feared that the Trump administration could send federal agents to polling places in immigrant communities.

Mr. Trump, who has voted by mail twice this year, has claimed that absentee voting is rife with fraud. He and his administration said in July, without evidence, that California and three other states had allowed about 278,000 noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

California’s Democratic leaders said they were responding to a spate of unusual challenges from Mr. Trump, and local officials aligned with him. Mr. Newsom signed the bills in Los Angeles at the Japanese American National Museum, where Border Patrol agents showed up outside a rally the governor held last summer.

Mr. Trump signed an executive order in March that sought to restrict the use of mail ballots. And earlier this year, Chad Bianco, the Republican sheriff in Riverside County, seized more than 650,000 ballots that voters had cast last year because he said he was investigating a discrepancy in the count. California challenged both actions in court. The Supreme Court on Monday sided with California and other Democratic-led states by blocking Mr. Trump’s plan to restrict voting by mail.

The new state laws add small but meaningful protections to California’s ability to prevent outside involvement in its ballot process, said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University who worked on voting rights for the Biden administration.

“There’s a vigilante mood afoot,” Mr. Levitt said. “This acts as a little bit of a deterrent for people who are cosplaying election officials.”

Shannon Grove, a Republican state senator who voted against the bills, said she believed one of the laws would allow criminal charges against U.S. Postal Service workers who handle ballots as a routine part of their job. Under that bill, it would be a misdemeanor for anyone in charge of a mail ballot to interfere with delivering it to a voter.

“This is about the postal workers, and that’s pretty bold,” she said.

In a brief interview last month, Mr. Newsom said the legislation wasn’t aimed at prosecuting postal workers who are doing their jobs properly.

The bills are targeted at those “carrying out illegal activity or illegal orders and directives,” Mr. Newsom said. “With these enhanced sanctions, if you break the law we’re going to hold you accountable, and it doesn’t matter who you are.”

Among the other bills that Mr. Newsom signed are two that took aim at “deepfake” ads generated by A.I. that mimic a politician’s voice or appearance to deceive voters.

In 2024, voters in New Hampshire received a voice message that was made to sound like President Joseph R. Biden Jr. urging them not to vote. That same year, an online ad imitated the voice of Vice President Kamala Harris saying Mr. Biden was senile.

California passed legislation cracking down on deepfake political ads that year, but it was later blocked by courts for violating free speech. The new legislation takes a narrower approach meant to strengthen it against constitutional challenges.

Mr. Newsom also signed a bill that could accelerate California’s notoriously slow process for counting votes.

It calls for election officials to tell people how to vote early, which reduces the glut of envelopes that arrive on Election Day. It also requires informing voters that they can submit mail ballots at a polling place. Doing so allows election officials to count ballots faster by eliminating the envelopes that are cumbersome to process.

Most election-related bills relied on Democratic support to pass, but the legislation to encourage early voting and in-person submission of ballots had sweeping bipartisan support.

Rick Hasen, an election law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said he was skeptical that California would be successful in stopping officials from the U.S. Department of Justice if they tried to collect ballots during an election, a scenario that has not occurred in modern times.

But, he said, the laws could be enforced against state and local officials. The state has already sued Mr. Bianco, and the parties in that case are awaiting a decision from the California Supreme Court.

item.title: Judy Gumbo, Who Found Freedom as a Yippie, Dies at 83
item.description:
Judy Gumbo, a key member of the leftist, anti-establishment Yippies who poked fun at the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, protested the Vietnam War in a Vietcong costume in Moscow, and was a target of F.B.I. surveillance and break-ins, died on Sept. 14 in Berkeley, Calif. She was 83.

Her daughter, Jessica Epstein, said she died of dementia in a memory care facility.

From the late 1960s to the early 1970s, the Yippies — formally the Youth International Party — mocked institutional figures with political satire and street theater to stop the Vietnam War and end other injustices.

“I am an original Yippie,” Ms. Gumbo wrote in her autobiography, “Yippie Girl: Exploits in Protest and Defeating the FBI” (2022). “A Yippie is a politicized hippie, a protester who has been hit over the head by a cop — and woke up.”

Ms. Gumbo was not as well known as Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, two of the party’s founders, but she was “an integral Yippie,” Nancy Kurshan, a Yippie who was Mr. Rubin’s partner for a while, said in an interview.

A few days before the Democratic convention, Ms. Gumbo was part of the contingent — which included her boyfriend and future husband, Stew Albert, a founder of the Yippies; Mr. Rubin; and the folk singer Phil Ochs — that drove to a farm to buy the 150-pound pig they brought to Civic Center in Chicago.

After a quick speech by a spokesman named Super Joel Yippie nominating Pigasus for president, Chicago police officers arrested seven Yippies for disorderly conduct and confiscated the pig. Fearing deportation to her native Canada if she had been arrested, Ms. Gumbo stayed on the sidelines, raising the $300 to bail out the jailed Yippies.

She viewed the riotous demonstrations outside the convention as the equivalent of a “live action antiwar documentary” and was thrilled that she had hit a police cruiser with a jar of “Yippie purple” paint.

“No girlie throw for me, I had hit what I had aimed for!” she wrote.

In a 2024 oral history of the convention riots in The New York Times, she recalled seeing officers beat protesters.

“It was scary, but I don’t remember the scary as much as I remember the empowerment,” she said. “The feeling of, ‘We are doing the right thing.’ ”

In 1969, when Mr. Rubin, Mr. Hoffman and five other defendants — the Chicago 7 — were tried in federal court for inciting a riot during the convention, Ms. Gumbo was named “conspiracy trial office manager” by William Kunstler, one of the defense lawyers.

Her job was traditional woman’s work: answering phones and handing out mail. She also retyped each day’s trial transcript, and then mimeographed it to produce enough copies to mail to national and foreign news outlets.

The Yippies were a patriarchal organization, said Ms. Kurshan, the author of a memoir, “Levitating the Pentagon and Other Uplifting Stories: A Life of Activism” (2026).

“Sometimes, we were invisible,” Ms. Kurshan said.

But in early 1970, Ms. Gumbo got a role in the forefront when a North Vietnamese delegation sent a message to the trial office wanting to meet members of the Chicago 7 in Montreal. The trial had not ended — and leaving for Canada might have meant violating the defendants’ bail — so Ms. Gumbo went instead.

“For peace activists like me to meet North Vietnamese — who our protest movement considered heroes — was the crown jewel in the pantheon of antiwar privilege,” she wrote in her book.

While there, she began a monthslong affair with Do Xuan Oanh, a poet and composer who headed the delegation.

The meeting led to Ms. Gumbo’s trip to Hanoi in May 1970, accompanied by Ms. Kurshan and Genie Plamondon, the minister of internal affairs for the radical White Panther Party. While there, Mr. Oanh handed Ms. Gumbo an envelope filled with 143 letters from American prisoners of war.

The next month, the three women flew to Moscow, where they dressed as Vietcong — black silk pajamas, conical hats and sandals — and gathered outside the United States Embassy to protest the war.

For about 30 minutes, they chanted and carried signs that declared, “We Are the Americong” and “Ho Chi Minh. The N.L.F. Is Gonna Win” — references to the Communist leader of North Vietnam and the National Liberation Front, whose guerrilla fighters were known as the Vietcong.

A small crowd of onlookers, embassy officials and Western media watched the women’s demonstration before it was peacefully broken up by a Soviet police officer. Photographs of the protest were seen in newspapers around the world.

Judith Lee Clavir was born in Toronto on June 25, 1943. Her father, Leo, was a film distributor who imported Soviet films and also was a game show producer. Her mother, Harriet (Kamman) Clavir, ran the home but was also an alcoholic.

“We were both Jewish and ‘godless’ Communists as the far right likes to claim,” she wrote in her memoir. “Instead of synagogue, our rituals took place in front of bookshelves, my atheistic family’s holy of holies.”

In 1965, she received a bachelor’s degree in sociology from the University of Toronto. Two years later, she was in graduate studies there when she attended a sociology conference in San Francisco and was enraptured by the free love philosophy expressed by one of the attendees.

She soon moved to Berkeley, where she met Mr. Albert — one of the Yippies’ founders — and was hired at The Berkeley Barb, an underground newspaper, to sell classified sex ads.

In 1968, while in a car with Mr. Albert and his close friend Eldridge Cleaver, the Black Panther, Mr. Cleaver referred to her as “Mrs. Stew.” She objected, saying she was nobody’s “Mrs.,” which led Mr. Cleaver to call her Gumbo. She loved it

Her activities with the Yippies attracted the scrutiny of the F.B.I. in its hunt for radicals. The agency, which viewed her as “dangerous to the internal security of the United States,” according to a document in its files, followed her, broke into the cabin she shared with Mr. Albert in the Catskills several times (partly in futile searches for fugitives) and placed homing devices in her cars.

In 1976, Ms. Gumbo and Mr. Albert sued the F.B.I. and Attorney General Edward H. Levi for illegal surveillance activities and three years later received a settlement of $20,000.

In the years after the Yippies faded, Ms. Gumbo taught sociology at SUNY New Paltz, Mills College, in Oakland, Calif., and the University of Oregon. She later worked as a fund-raiser for Planned Parenthood in Portland, Ore. She received a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of Toronto in 1975.

Her first marriage, to David Hemblen, an actor, ended in divorce. Mr. Albert, whom she married in 1977, died in 2006. She was married to David Dobkin, a financial planner, from 2009 until his death in 2014. They walked down the aisle to a klezmer musician playing “The Internationale,” the socialist and Communist anthem.

In 2017, she married Arthur Eckstein, a historian at the University of Maryland who wrote “Bad Moon Rising: How the Weather Underground Beat the FBI and Lost the Revolution” (2016).

In addition to her husband and her daughter, from her second marriage, Ms. Gumbo is survived by a grandson.

Ms. Gumbo met Professor Eckstein after contacting him to complain about parts of his book. Their romance started with emails and progressed in phone conversations and FaceTime sessions.

“I never thought I would say this,” Ms. Gumbo told The San Francisco Chronicle in 2017, “but I am grateful to the F.B.I. for bringing us together.”

item.title: News Outlets Express Solidarity After Trump Bars Some Reporters
item.description:
Many major media outlets and some high-profile Democrats panned President Trump’s abrupt decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

Mr. Trump acted on his latest barrage of threats against the press on Saturday morning, when reporters for the outlets were denied access to the White House and had their badges confiscated.

On Friday evening, Mr. Trump had accused the three outlets of running “purposely negative stories” that were untrue, though he provided no details. The Trump administration has not said what led to his decision, which many First Amendment groups called unconstitutional and unlikely to survive a court challenge.

Condemnation from leading news outlets was nearly universal, including from many that compete directly with CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

“No news organization — or person — should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use,” said Lauren Easton, a spokeswoman for The Associated Press, which filed suit over restrictions that Mr. Trump tried to impose on its White House access last year.

The New York Times, The Washington Post and press associations also released statements calling the ban an attack on free speech and the free press.

Journalists at Fox News have also taken issue with the ban. One Fox contributor, Ari Fleischer, said conservatives should challenge liberal reporters. “Argue and defeat them,” he said. “Don’t ban them. Or one day they’ll ban us.” Another contributor, Jonathan Turley, said that “barring disfavored media from the White House is a terrible precedent and practice.”

Jacqui Heinrich, a Fox News anchor and the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, said on social media that the right to First Amendment protections “does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage.”

“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Ms. Heinrich added. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”

Democrats pounced on Mr. Trump’s ban as an attempt to hide his administration’s shortcomings and to distract voters from other issues. They pointed out that Republicans were heading into a challenging election cycle with high inflation and an unpopular war with Iran started by Mr. Trump, whose support in the polls has sagged.

“Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader, said on social media. “This is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth.”

Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on the news media to boycott the White House if Mr. Trump “keeps violating press freedom.” Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said Mr. Trump was censoring the press and trying to “hide his failures.” Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont said that Mr. Trump wanted to “control the flow of information and silence media that might hold them accountable.”

“We will not allow Trump to undermine the First Amendment, the Constitution and our democracy,” Mr. Sanders said on social media. “We will not accept authoritarianism.”

High-ranking Republicans and members of the Trump administration mostly remained quiet on Saturday. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has tried to restrict reporters’ access to the Pentagon, said he “fully supports” a ban on some outlets that he and Mr. Trump have labeled “fake news” for negative coverage.

“They endangered our troops with false stories, leaks, and trafficked in fiction and lies about the President,” Mr. Hegseth said, without providing examples or evidence.

Benny Johnson, a right-wing podcaster, also celebrated the decision to block certain outlets from the White House and pointed out that Mr. Trump had been banned from social media platforms after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol by his supporters.

“No one is infringing on their ability to do reporting,” Mr. Johnson said in a social media post.

The campaign of former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican running with Mr. Trump’s backing for a competitive Senate seat in Michigan, appeared to distance itself from the president’s decision.

Mr. Rogers “held a press conference just this morning with invites out to each of those outlets,” Alyssa Brouillet, a spokeswoman for his campaign, said in a statement. “That tells you where he stands.”

Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator, was more explicit.

“Unpopular opinion in my parts, but it’s insane and a very slippery slope to kick media outlets you don’t like out of the White House,” Ms. McCain said.

Olivia Diaz and Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Faced Loss After Loss. He Then Turned to a Familiar Target: The Press.
item.description:
President Trump’s grabs for power kept falling short, and he appeared ready to turn to a familiar target.

He had relentlessly pressured the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts to affix his name to its facade, only to be blocked by the courts. He had gone to extraordinary lengths to bully the Federal Reserve into lowering interest rates, only to have his handpicked Fed chairman join his colleagues in voting unanimously to raise borrowing costs.

Despite his attempts to talk his way out of it, the war against Iran continues to be immensely unpopular with Americans concerned with Mr. Trump’s handling of the economy and high gasoline prices. The Supreme Court, including justices he appointed, blocked Mr. Trump’s attempts to restrict mail-in voting.

And with the midterm elections looming, the president’s political authority appears to be ebbing after years in which he dominated not just his party but also the national discourse.

So after these losses, an increasingly frustrated Mr. Trump, seeking to change the subject, has turned to a new assault on his preferred foe: the news media.

The White House on Saturday moved ahead with Mr. Trump’s surprise announcement banning journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, an escalation in Mr. Trump’s long battle with the press.

But it also fits a pattern for Mr. Trump when he faces a political quagmire, according to former government officials and civil rights organizations: He seeks to change the narrative by mobilizing the government to crack down on those willing to question his power.

“He thinks that he can bully anyone or any entity into doing whatever he wants and he’s seen it work out for himself with the entire Republican Party bending the knee to him,” said Sarah Matthews, a deputy press secretary in Mr. Trump’s first term. “He is facing pushback from the courts, the Fed, people in his own party, and he’s lashing out.”

Mr. Trump has long insulted and derided the news media and sought to use the courts to crush critical coverage. But surrounded by like-minded loyalists in his return to the White House, he has gone beyond harsh statements or lawsuits.

The administration has stripped funding from public television and radio. The Pentagon fired the editor and publisher of its traditionally independent newspaper, Stars and Stripes. Journalists at the organization claimed the administration ousted them because they wrote about the worsening conditions inside a Navy aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East.

He has pushed the government to revoke the licenses of broadcasters that air negative coverage or commentary of him. He has moved to target the tax status of liberal groups, monitor online speech and deny visas to those expressing views he does not like.

It was Mr. Trump who on Friday said he was imposing the ban, which caught some White House officials by surprise and occurred while his chief of staff was out of town, because he did not like the coverage of the three news outlets. And he indicated he would lift his ban if they succumbed to his will.

“Maybe they can get better and we’d like to have them in,” Mr. Trump said in what appeared to translate to an ultimatum for the news outlets: Give me better coverage and I will let you in the White House.

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Mr. Trump added. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house.”

First Amendment experts and civil rights organizations said the Constitution says differently. Mr. Trump’s ban appeared clearly unconstitutional because it would punish news organizations for the content of their reporting, experts said.

Derrick Johnson, the president of the NAACP, said Mr. Trump was also trying to redirect attention.

“Donald Trump has a problem with the public knowing the truth, and that’s because the truth isn’t favorable to him,” Mr. Johnson said. “Soaring gas prices aren’t favorable to him. The Epstein files aren’t favorable to him. A weakening economy isn’t favorable to him. The only thing that is favorable to him is the public believing his lies — and that is only possible if he controls the narrative.”

The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Trump’s efforts to crack down on dissent and the news media have not helped address concerns of voters or Republicans staring down significant losses in the November elections. Polling has found a majority of American adult voters believe Mr. Trump hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems.

Douglas Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee, said more Americans were also noticing Mr. Trump’s anger manifesting into lashing out. Indeed, after a federal judge barred the Kennedy Center from honoring Mr. Trump by attaching his name to the institution’s exterior, Mr. Trump threatened to cancel a planned $257 million renovation for the building.

Images captured through the windows of Air Force One later showed President Trump reviewing a poster with the title “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED,” fueling speculation he could destroy an institution he could not put his stamp on.

Many Republicans wish Mr. Trump focused as much on policies that would address the economic concerns among their supporters, Mr. Heye said.

“He certainly uses brash tactics to take over news cycles. I would argue that quite often these are unhelpful to him,” Mr. Heye said. “We are 45 days ahead from the election and what are we talking about this week and going into next week? Nothing about Donald Trump’s plan to lower prices.”

item.title: A.I. Gone Rogue? Trump Proposes Not New Rules but an ‘A.I. Force.’
item.description:
President Trump is so enamored of the Space Force, a military command he created in his first term, that he keeps its flag by his desk in the Oval Office. He took personal interest in the design of its uniforms, which bear close resemblance to those of Galactic Empire officers in “Star Wars.”

On Saturday, Mr. Trump proposed a follow-on to Space Force: a new “A.I. Force.” But he left to earthbound speculation what, exactly, it was supposed to do.

Mr. Trump cast his announcement — along with his promise to appoint a new A.I. “Czar” for the White House — as an effort to boost the A.I. industry, saying “we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it.”

In the roiling debate in Washington over regulating frontier A.I. models and the companies that produce them, or slowing down development until the mystery is solved about the summer in which A.I. agents went rogue, Mr. Trump continues to side with the “accelerationists,” who call for the government to stay out of the way.

Mr. Trump, in his social media post, compared warnings about A.I. with warnings about global warming and conspiracies that he said were created by “Radical Left Democrats,” ignoring concerns about A.I. shared by many Republicans.

Mr. Trump did not make clear whether he envisioned the new A.I. Force as a military command or a civilian agency or department. White House officials did not respond to an email seeking clarification.

And at a moment when the battle is on in Washington over the prospect of federal oversight of frontier models and Chinese-developed open source alternatives, he did not explain how the A.I. Force would fit in as private sector rivals race for even more powerful A.I. models.

Mr. Trump’s posting was cheered by his last A.I. czar, the venture capitalist David Sacks.

“President Trump understands the media hoax cycle better than anyone else,” he wrote on X. “That is why he is refusing the ‘pause’ that Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren are demanding. A pause would not make America safer. It would hand the frontier to China.”

This is not the first time that Mr. Trump has called for the creation of new institutions to take on a technological challenge.

In his first term, after a meeting with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, he declared that the two men would create a joint cyberspace force to fight cybercrime. His national security aides said they were mystified about why the United States would join forces with a primary rival for power in the cyber arena. The idea was quietly dropped.

In this case, there are already institutions aimed at overseeing artificial intelligence issues.

United States Cyber Command is actively experimenting with frontier models, including Anthropic’s powerful Mythos, to find vulnerabilities in adversary computer networks, making them more ripe for attack. It is also trying to help patch previously undiscovered vulnerabilities in critical U.S. infrastructure systems.

That is also the task of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, part of the Department of Homeland Security. But its personnel has been gutted since Mr. Trump came to office, in part because of the agency’s role in declaring that the 2020 presidential election was among the best-run in modern times. It challenged his arguments that the vote had been rigged.

On Friday, former President Barack Obama for the first time publicly criticized Mr. Trump over his approach to A.I., saying that the president was setting the country back at an important moment, warning that the technology could “deeply affect our health and our safety.”

“There’s no replacement for an effective, government regulatory structure,” Mr. Obama said at an event at Colgate University in Hamilton, N.Y. “And the challenge we have is that, obviously, we have a president currently that has said that’s for losers.”

The United States, he added, is facing “a gap, at least of a couple of years” while Mr. Trump is in office, because of a federal government “that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — of putting together a serious regulatory framework.”

Last week, Mr. Obama urged Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the top House Democrat, to develop a clear agenda for the party on A.I. But on Friday, Mr. Obama also turned his focus to voters.

“I would encourage voters to pay attention to this,” Mr. Obama said at Colgate. “If somebody does not have a serious plan for how to deal with this, then they’re not meeting the moment, and you should probably look for somebody else.”

Neither party has united around a defined position on A.I. regulation, and neither has claimed a clear advantage with voters on the issue, according to polls.

item.title: Hiker Dies After Lightning Strikes ‘Tin Shack’ on Utah Mountain
item.description:
A 19-year-old man died on Friday in a lightning storm while huddled with nine other people inside a metal structure atop a mountain in Utah, the authorities said.

The man was at the summit of the peak, Mount Timpanogos, when scattered storm cells moved through late Thursday and early Friday, the authorities said.

The man, who has not been publicly identified, was with the others inside a structure known as the Tin Shack when the storm struck, said Sgt. Ray Ormond, the public information officer with the Utah County Sheriff’s Office.

The shack, a well-known spot atop the peak, was built out of steel in 1927 as a lookout house, according to The Daily Herald in Provo, Utah.

Lightning struck it, leaving nine people with minor injuries, Sergeant Ormond said. Hikers alerted the authorities at about 6 a.m.

The 19-year-old man was critically injured and was pronounced dead on the mountain, the sheriff’s office said in a news release.

There were 517 lightning-related deaths from 2006 through last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Nearly 90 percent of people who are struck by lightning survive, the C.D.C said.

The storm system on Friday was not abnormal, said Darren Van Cleave, the meteorologist-in-charge at the National Weather Service office in Salt Lake City.

The severe weather arrived during Utah’s monsoon season and in conjunction with a jet of moisture from the west, Mr. Van Cleave said, adding that each cell that passed through the area had been filled with lightning.

“It was a very electrically active day,” he said.

Mount Timpanogos, which is more than 11,740 feet tall and sits about 50 miles southeast of Salt Lake City, features two main routes to the top, each a little more than 14 miles round-trip, said Jim Steenburgh, a professor of atmospheric science at the University of Utah.

Many local residents trek to the summit to bask in the expansive views of the Utah Valley, often at either sunrise or sunset, he said. The popular climb offers glimpses of wildlife and waterfalls while ascending steep terrain.

Hikers climb on an exposed ridge line to reach the peak, he said, leaving them few places to take shelter until a storm passes.

Experts recommend that recreationists check the weather forecast before heading out. Conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, the sheriff’s office said, noting that “lightning can strike well away from the main area of rainfall.”

If thunder is rumbling nearby, the authorities advise moving away from exposed ridgelines and heading for a safe location. People should also refrain from touching materials that can conduct electricity, such as metal, utility lines, water and plumbing, according to the C.D.C.

Small, exposed structures cannot protect a person from lightning.

“The safest locations are substantial, fully enclosed buildings or an enclosed, hard-topped vehicle,” the sheriff’s office said.
